keyVerseText: And Jehu slept with his fathers: and they buried him in Samaria. And Jehoahaz his son reigned in his stead.
rootMeaning: The name יְהוֹאָחָז (Yᵉhôwʼâchâz) is derived from two Hebrew elements: יְהֹוָה (Jehovah), the personal name of God meaning 'the existing One,' and the verb אָחַז, meaning 'to seize' or 'to grasp.' Thus, the literal meaning of the name is 'Jehovah has seized' or 'the Lord has grasped.' This root sense conveys a powerful image of God's active involvement and sovereign hold over the individual bearing this name, going beyond a mere label to express divine possession or intervention.
usageInScripture: The word יְהוֹאָחָז appears twenty times in Scripture, primarily as a proper name for three distinct Israelite kings—two from Judah and one from Israel—and also as a father of Josiah's chronicler. The dominant translation is simply 'Jehoahaz,' with occasional variants such as 'of Jehoahaz' or 'And Jehoahaz,' reflecting its consistent use as a personal name. This consistency highlights the significance of the name as an identifier of historical figures through whom God's sovereign will was manifested in Israel's history.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, the name יְהוֹאָחָז reminds believers that God is sovereign and actively 'grips' or 'seizes' His people and their circumstances. It underscores the biblical truth that God is not distant or passive but intimately involved in the unfolding of history and the lives of His servants. For the Christian faith, this name points forward to the ultimate grasp of God in Christ, who holds all things together and secures salvation. Recognizing God's active hand in the lives of those named יְהוֹאָחָז encourages trust in His providential control and faithfulness.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Kings 10:35, the verse states, 'And Jehu slept with his fathers: and they buried him in Samaria. And Jehoahaz his son reigned in his stead.' Here, the name Jehoahaz signals the continuation of God's sovereign plan through a new generation of leadership. The meaning 'Jehovah has seized' enriches this transition by implying that God’s authority and purpose remain firmly held even as kings pass away, reminding readers that divine sovereignty governs the rise and fall of earthly rulers.
